column1: #tags column:3
The three axioms of probability?
column2: Nonnegativity \(P(A) \ge 0\); normalization \(P(\Omega) = 1\); additivity for disjoint events. Everything else (complements, inclusion–exclusion, the union bound) is derived.

column1: Inclusion–exclusion for two events?
column2: \(P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B)\): adding the two counts the overlap twice.

column1: The union bound, and when it is tight?
column2: \(P(A_1 \cup \dots \cup A_n) \le \sum P(A_i)\), for any events, with no independence needed. Tight when the events are rare and nearly disjoint; useless once the sum nears 1.

column1: Probability that \(n\) independent bits at BER \(p\) contain an error?
column2: \(1 - (1 - p)^n \approx 1 - e^{-np} \approx np\) when \(np \ll 1\). Compute it as \(-\mathrm{expm1}(n\,\mathrm{log1p}(-p))\) to avoid cancellation.

column1: At BER 1e-12 on a 32 Gb/s lane, how often does an error occur?
column2: 0.032 errors per second: one every 31.25 s on average. Rare per bit is not rare per second.

column1: Probability of exactly \(k\) errors in \(n\) independent bits?
column2: \(\binom{n}{k}p^k(1 - p)^{n - k}\): the number of patterns times the probability of each (the binomial distribution).

column1: Birthday problem: when do random IDs from N values start colliding?
column2: Around \(k \approx \sqrt{N}\): \(P(\text{collision}) \approx 1 - e^{-k(k - 1)/(2N)}\). With 16-bit IDs, 302 devices make a collision more likely than not.

column1: Definition of conditional probability, and its meaning?
column2: \(P(A \mid B) = P(A \cap B)/P(B)\): the fraction of the outcomes where \(B\) happened that also have \(A\), a renormalized probability law on \(B\).

column1: Total probability theorem?
column2: For a partition \(B_1, \dots, B_m\): \(P(A) = \sum_iP(B_i)P(A \mid B_i)\). A fab's yield is the share-weighted average of its lines' yields.

column1: Bayes' rule, and its odds form?
column2: \(P(A \mid B) = P(A)P(B \mid A)/P(B)\). Posterior odds = likelihood ratio × prior odds.

column1: What is the base-rate effect?
column2: A test with a small false-positive rate still gives mostly false alarms when the condition is rare, because the false-positive rate applies to the large healthy majority. A 99%/1% alarm on a 0.1% fault rate is right only about 9% of the time.

column1: MAP versus ML detection?
column2: MAP picks the symbol with the largest posterior \(P(s \mid y) \propto P(s)P(y \mid s)\) and minimizes error probability. ML ignores priors; the two agree when priors are equal. With skewed priors MAP can ignore the data entirely.

column1: Definition of independence, and what it does not imply?
column2: \(P(A \cap B) = P(A)P(B)\). Pairwise independence does not imply mutual independence: two fair bits and their XOR are pairwise independent but jointly determined.

column1: What is conditional independence? Give an EE example.
column2: Independent once a third quantity is known. Two tests of the same die can be independent given its true state yet dependent overall, because both reflect that state.

column1: Reliability of series and parallel systems?
column2: Series: \(\prod R_i\) (10 parts at 0.99 give 0.904). Parallel: \(1 - \prod(1 - R_i)\) (two at 0.99 give 0.9999).

column1: TMR reliability and its break-even?
column2: \(3R^2 - 2R^3\) with a perfect voter. Better than one module only for \(R > 0.5\); an imperfect voter also caps the useful range from above.

column1: Common-mode (beta-factor) failures in a duplicated system?
column2: \(P(\text{both fail}) \approx \beta q + ((1 - \beta)q)^2\). Even β = 0.1 at q = 0.01 makes the risk about 11 times the independent \(q^2\).

column1: Downtime per year for three, four and five nines?
Williams–Brown defect level?
column2: \(\text{DL} = 1 - Y^{1 - T} \approx (1 - T)\ln(1/Y)\) for yield \(Y\) and fault coverage \(T\). DPPM scales with the untested fraction: each tenfold cut needs ten times fewer untested faults.

column1: Why does better yield lower DPPM with the same test?
column2: Defect level is \(P(\text{bad} \mid \text{pass})\); higher yield lowers the prior \(P(\text{bad})\), so fewer bad dies reach the tester to escape (Bayes).

column1: How many error-free bits show BER < p at 95% confidence?
Serial-link BER targets (as of Nov 2026)?
column2: PCIe Gen 1–5 (NRZ): \(10^{-12}\). PCIe 6.0 (PAM4): first-bit error rate \(10^{-6}\) with FEC, CRC and retry. Ethernet 400G/800G/1.6T: \(10^{-13}\) at the MAC [R-059].

column1: What does zero failures in 3 lots × 77 units of qualification prove?
column2: That the defective fraction is below about 1% at 90% confidence (LTPD 1). It cannot demonstrate ppm quality: that would take hundreds of thousands of units [R-061].

column1: PMF, PDF and CDF: how are they related?
column2: PMF \(p_X(k) = P(X = k)\) for discrete \(X\); PDF \(f_X\) is a density, \(P(a < X \le b) = \int_a^b f_X\); CDF \(F_X(x) = P(X \le x)\) is the running sum or integral. \(f_X = dF_X/dx\).

column1: Why can a PDF exceed 1 but a PMF cannot?
column2: A PMF value is a probability. A PDF value is probability per unit of \(x\); only its integral over an interval is a probability.

column1: Binomial PMF and when it applies?
column2: \(\binom nk p^k(1-p)^{n-k}\): the number of successes in \(n\) independent trials with the same probability \(p\). Mean \(np\).

column1: Geometric distribution: PMF and use?
column2: Trials until the first success: \(P(K = k) = (1-q)^{k-1}q\). Retransmissions, link-training attempts. \(P(K > k) = (1-q)^k\).

column1: Poisson PMF, and when does it approximate the binomial?
column2: \(P(k) = \lambda^k e^{-\lambda}/k!\), mean and variance λ. It is the binomial's limit for large \(n\), small \(p\), fixed \(\lambda = np\); the error is at most about \(np^2\) (Le Cam).

column1: Poisson yield model?
column2: With defect density \(D_0\) and die area \(A\), defects per die are Poisson with \(\lambda = AD_0\), so yield (no defect) is \(e^{-AD_0}\).

column1: What is a FIT?
column2: One failure per \(10^9\) device-hours. Rates in FIT add for parts in series. 1000 FIT is about 0.9% per year [R-064].

column1: Convert a FIT rate into a probability over time \(t\)?
column2: Constant rate \(r = \text{FIT}\times10^{-9}\) per hour: \(P(\text{fail by } t) = 1 - e^{-rt} \approx rt\) when \(rt \ll 1\).

column1: Exponential distribution: where does it come from?
column2: The waiting time to the first event of a constant-rate process: \(P(T > t) = e^{-rt}\). Mean \(1/r\). Gaps of a Poisson process are exponential.

column1: Memoryless property?
column2: \(P(T > s + t \mid T > s) = P(T > t)\): a survivor is as good as new. Only the exponential (continuous) and geometric (discrete) have it. False for wear-out.

column1: What does an MTTF of \(10^6\) hours mean?
column2: A constant failure rate of 1000 FIT, about 0.9% per year. It is not a 114-year life; wear-out ends real life much sooner.

column1: Q-function definition?
column2: \(Q(x) = P(Z > x)\) for standard normal \(Z\) \(= \tfrac12\operatorname{erfc}(x/\sqrt2)\). \(P(X > a) = Q((a - \mu)/\sigma)\).

column1: Within ±1σ, ±2σ, ±3σ of a Gaussian mean?

column2: 5.998, 7.034, 7.941: the σ of margin needed.

column1: Bounds on Q(x) for large x?
column2: \(\frac{x}{1 + x^2}\phi(x) < Q(x) < \phi(x)/x\) with \(\phi(x) = e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\), and \(Q(x) \le \tfrac12e^{-x^2/2}\). The tail falls like \(e^{-x^2/2}\).

column1: BER of a binary ±A signal in Gaussian noise σ, threshold at 0?
What does 1 dB of lost signal cost near BER \(10^{-12}\)?
column2: \(A/\sigma\) falls from 7.034 to 6.269, and the BER rises about 181-fold to \(1.8\times10^{-10}\).

column1: Dual-Dirac total jitter formula?
column2: \(TJ(\text{BER}) = DJ(\delta\delta) + 2Q_{\text{BER}}\sigma_{RJ}\), with \(2Q_{\text{BER}} = 14.069\) at \(10^{-12}\) and 15.883 at \(10^{-15}\) (transition density 1/2) [R-063].

column1: How do independent random jitters combine?
column2: In quadrature: \(\sigma = \sqrt{\sigma_1^2 + \sigma_2^2}\). Attack the largest term first.

column1: Eye opening at a target BER?
column2: \(1\,\text{UI} - TJ(\text{BER})\). At 32 GT/s (31.25 ps) with DJ 8 ps and RJ 1.2 ps rms: 6.367 ps at \(10^{-12}\).

column1: Six Sigma's 3.4 ppm: where does it come from?
column2: Limits at ±6σ with the mean assumed to drift 1.5σ: \(Q(4.5) = 3.4\times10^{-6}\). The centered ±6σ figure is 2 ppb. The 1.5σ shift is a convention, not a law [R-065].

column1: When does a Gaussian tail model fail?
column2: When tails are bounded or heavier than Gaussian: crosstalk, interference, bursty or clustered errors. Fit the model near the BER it is used at, and distrust extrapolation many decades out.

column1: Expectation of a discrete and a continuous random variable?
column2: \(\mathbb{E}[X] = \sum_k k\,p_X(k)\) or \(\int x f_X(x)\,dx\): the probability-weighted average, the balance point of the distribution, and the long-run average of many trials.

column1: Expectation of a function \(g(X)\)?
column2: \(\mathbb{E}[g(X)] = \sum g(k)p_X(k)\) or \(\int g(x)f_X(x)\,dx\). You do not need the distribution of \(g(X)\).

column1: Does \(\mathbb{E}[X + Y] = \mathbb{E}[X] + \mathbb{E}[Y]\) need independence?
column2: No. Linearity of expectation always holds. Variances add only for uncorrelated (e.g. independent) terms.

column1: The indicator trick?
column2: Write a count as a sum of indicators \(I_{A_i}\); then \(\mathbb{E}[N] = \sum P(A_i)\), exact even when the events are correlated (expected good dies, colliding ID pairs).

column1: MTTF from the reliability function?
column2: \(\text{MTTF} = \int_0^\infty R(t)\,dt\). Two exponential parts in parallel: \(1.5/r\), not \(2/r\). TMR: \(5/(6r)\), below a single part.

column1: Variance: definition and computing form?
column2: \(\operatorname{Var}(X) = \mathbb{E}[(X - \mu)^2] = \mathbb{E}[X^2] - \mu^2\). \(\operatorname{Var}(aX + b) = a^2\operatorname{Var}(X)\).

column1: Mean and variance: binomial, Poisson, geometric?
column2: Binomial \(np\), \(np(1-p)\). Poisson λ, λ. Geometric (trials to first success, success prob. \(q\)): \(1/q\), \((1-q)/q^2\).

column1: Mean and variance: uniform, exponential, Gaussian?
column2: Uniform width \(w\): midpoint, \(w^2/12\). Exponential rate \(r\): \(1/r\), \(1/r^2\) (σ equals the mean). Gaussian: μ, σ².

column1: Total power of a random voltage in terms of its moments?
column2: \(\mathbb{E}[V^2] = (\mathbb{E}[V])^2 + \operatorname{Var}(V)\): total = DC + AC power (into 1 Ω). RMS is \(\sqrt{\mathbb{E}[V^2]}\); AC RMS is σ.

column1: Why do noise powers add but noise voltages do not?
column2: For independent zero-mean signals the cross term \(\mathbb{E}[XY] = 0\), so \(\mathbb{E}[(X+Y)^2] = \mathbb{E}[X^2] + \mathbb{E}[Y^2]\).

column1: Change-of-variables formula for \(Y = g(X)\)?
column2: \(f_Y(y) = \sum_i f_X(x_i)/|g'(x_i)|\) over all \(x_i\) with \(g(x_i) = y\). The CDF method \(F_Y(y) = P(g(X) \le y)\) always works.

column1: Density of noise power \(Y = X^2\), \(X \sim \mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2)\)?
column2: \(f_Y(y) = e^{-y/(2\sigma^2)}/(\sigma\sqrt{2\pi y})\) (chi-square, 1 degree of freedom). Mean σ², standard deviation \(\sqrt2\sigma^2\).

column1: Log-normal: median and mean of \(e^X\), \(X \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, s^2)\)?
column2: Median \(e^\mu\); mean \(e^{\mu + s^2/2}\). The mean exceeds the median: average leakage beats median-device leakage.

column1: Why is MOSFET leakage roughly log-normal across devices?
column2: Subthreshold current is exponential in \(V_{GS} - V_{TH}\) (\(\propto e^{-V_{TH}/(nV_T)}\)), and \(V_{TH}\) varies roughly Gaussian across devices.

column1: Markov and Chebyshev inequalities?
column2: Markov: \(P(X \ge a) \le \mathbb{E}[X]/a\) for \(X \ge 0\). Chebyshev: \(P(|X - \mu| \ge k\sigma) \le 1/k^2\): 11.1% at 3σ for any distribution, vs 0.27% for a Gaussian.

column1: Jensen's inequality and an EE example?
column2: For convex \(g\), \(\mathbb{E}[g(X)] \ge g(\mathbb{E}[X])\). Leakage at the average \(V_{TH}\), or failure rate at the average temperature, underestimates the average.

column1: Gaussian mean absolute value, and what an average-responding meter reads on noise?
column2: \(\mathbb{E}|X| = \sigma\sqrt{2/\pi} = 0.7979\sigma\). The meter (×1.1107) reads 0.8862σ: 1.05 dB low.

column1: PAPR of a sine; of a complex Gaussian (OFDM) at \(10^{-4}\)?
column2: Sine: 3.01 dB (crest factor √2). Complex Gaussian: power is exponential, PAPR \(= 10\log_{10}\ln(1/p)\) = 9.64 dB at \(10^{-4}\).

column1: Why must the PAPR of OFDM be quoted at a probability?
column2: Noise-like signals have no hard peak; the reported crest factor grows with capture length. Quote the CCDF level (e.g. at 0.01%).

column1: Measured crest factors: LTE downlink vs uplink (as of Nov 2026)?
column2: R&S: 20 MHz LTE downlink (OFDMA) 11.65 dB; SC-FDMA uplink 5.15–6.03 dB; WCDMA about 4 dB. Low PAPR is why uplinks use DFT-spread OFDM [R-066].

column1: ADC loading factor tradeoff?
column2: \(k = V_{FS}/\sigma\). Granular SNR \(= 6.02N + 4.77 - 20\log_{10}k\) dB falls with \(k\); clipping noise \(2[(1+k^2)Q(k) - k\phi(k)]\) falls with \(k\). Optimum about 3.9 (8 bits), 5.0 (12 bits).

column1: Class-B PA average efficiency with an OFDM signal backed off to its \(10^{-4}\) PAPR?
column2: About 29%, vs 78.5% (π/4) for a full-scale sine, in the ideal model \(\bar\eta = (\pi/4)\mathbb{E}[R^2]/(r_{\max}\mathbb{E}[R])\).
